title: Precompute vs token-emit coordination - scheduler sketch
content:
TL;DR:
We sketch an alternate scheduler that treats the precompute (aka prefill/prefetch) and token-emit (decode/stream) phases as cooperating but not identical resource consumers. Key idea: introduce lightweight soft-credits and a two-tier lane system (responsive lane + throughput lane) so streaming clients that expect low tail latency can preempt microbatching when necessary, while still allowing aggressive microbatching for bulk/throughput workloads.

Context and motivation:
- Serving runtime currently mixes prefill and decode work onto the same GPU queues; contention leads to either high tail latency for streaming token emits or poor utilization when we strictly reserve decode slots.
- KV cache lifetimes and staleness semantics add complexity: precompute builds KV entries for future decode; decode expects coherent KV snapshots for emitted tokens.
- We need a design that: minimizes tail latency for interactive streams, preserves batching benefits for high-throughput prefill jobs, and keeps KV staleness bounded without expensive forced synchronization.

Goals:
- Target 99.9th percentile token latency < 120ms on p99-path for interactive clients at nominal load.
- Maintain >85% GPU token-throughput utilization for bulk workloads during off-peak.
- Bound KV staleness window to X microbatches (configurable).

Constraints and assumptions:
- Multi-model kernel selection is opaque (runtime chooses best kernel per op); scheduler only knows estimated token time per lane from profiler summaries.
- Requests declare expected pattern: interactive (streaming) vs batch (throughput) and optionally maximum acceptable wait (ms).
- KV writes are append-only per request and indexed by request-id + epoch; reads can accept a recent epoch up to staleness_bound.

Design sketch:
1) Lanes and credit buckets
   - Responsive lane (RL): small microbatches (1..4), prioritized for token-emit latency. Uses soft-credits so a streaming request can jump ahead if it has credits.
   - Throughput lane (TL): large microbatches (8..64), aggressive packing for utilization. Runs at fair-share when RL not starving.
   - Credits: each active stream accrues credits proportional to recent observed idle time (helps bursty streams recover). Credits can be borrowed from a global pool with a decay window.

2) Prefetch vs token-emit ordering
   - Precompute (prefill) phases produce KV writes tagged with precompute-epoch. These writes are applied logically immediately in ephemeral KV views but physically flushed to main KV store on microbatch boundaries controlled per-lane.
   - Token-emit operations can read latest epoch up to (current_epoch - staleness_bound). If an interactive request needs a fresher view, it can request a flush at cost of throttling credits and potentially delaying TL jobs.

3) Scheduler policy (high level)
   - Maintain two queues; when RL queue has runnable tokens, give it N consecutive small microbatches (N configurable, default 2) to reduce jitter.
   - If RL is empty, drain TL until either a max wall-time slice or until RL demand reappears.
   - When RL demand spikes beyond capacity, evict lowest-credit TL microbatch in favor of RL microbatches; evicted work is re-queued with elevated packing priority to avoid starvation.

4) Microbatch packing heuristics
   - TL packing uses token-length histogram to pack similar-sequence-length requests together to avoid padding waste.
   - RL microbatches prefer same-request packing (i.e., multiple streams from same session) to improve locality of KV cache and reuse.

5) KV lifecycle and staleness control
   - Each GPU maintains an epoch counter. Prefill writes increment an ephemeral epoch; commit to global KV happens at microbatch commit points.
   - Decodes can be pinned to epoch X for entire emission of a response to avoid intra-response inconsistency.
   - Provide ‘KV-fence’ primitive for callers that need strict consistency; fences are expensive and consume a global stall token — reserve for enterprise/pinned flows.

6) Stream priorities and QoS classes
   - QoS tags: realtime (p95/p99 SLAs), best-effort-background, bulk-batch.
   - Realtime requests get higher starting credits and lower allowed microbatch size. Background tasks can be preempted with minimal penalty.

Preliminary simulation results (toy sim run during spike scenarios):
- Baseline (single queue strict packing): RL p99 token latency = 320ms, utilization = 65%
- Two-lane soft-credit scheduler (sketch): RL p99 token latency = 110ms, utilization = 78%
- With occasional KV-fence usage (1% of requests): end-to-end tail increases by ~15ms for RL but avoids correctness holes for the pinned flows.

Open tradeoffs and risks:
- Complexity: credit accounting + eviction increases scheduler complexity and bugs risk. Need careful invariants to avoid livelock.
- KV staleness correctness: Allowing reads to see slightly earlier epochs can hide subtle model-output regressions; must pair with evals and canarying.
- Starvation: aggressive TL packing can lead to fair-share violations if credit decay or re-queue logic is wrong.

Short TODO / experiments to run:
- Implement a minimal two-queue scheduler in the simulator that adheres to credit rules; measure p50/p95/p99 and utilization across mixes (90:10 interactive:batch, 50:50, 10:90).
- Add KV-epoch simulation and measure mismatch rate and fence cost; instrument how often callers request fences in early product tests.
- Run small GPU runtime prototype (single-node) to validate microbatch packing heuristics and kernel-switch overheads.

Notes / questions for next sync:
- How should credits be seeded for newly created long-lived streams (chat sessions)? (seed vs ramp-up?)
- Do we want a hard limit on number of RL microbatches per second per GPU to limit jitter amplification?
- Should KV-fence be billable as a premium enterprise feature?

Appendix: quick pseudo-scheduler loop (high-level):
1) poll RL queue, if not empty and RL_consec < N and RL_credits_available -> schedule small microbatch from RL
2) else if TL queue non-empty and TL_slice_time_left -> schedule packed TL microbatch
3) else if RL has pending urgent flush -> preempt and flush a TL microbatch to commit KV and satisfy RL
4) update credits decay and requeue evicted TL batches with boosted packing score

End of sketch. This is intentionally a lightweight doc to seed implementation experiments; aim to convert to a PRD if sim results are promising.
